title: Beyond the degree: Fertility outcomes of 'first in family' graduates
journal: Review of Economics of the Household
summary_en: Why do graduate women have fewer children than non-graduates? Using the 1970 British Cohort Study, the paper compares three groups: 'first in family' graduates (the first in their household to attend university), graduates with university-educated parents, and women who never attended. The fertility gap is driven almost entirely by the first-in-family group, mostly through higher childlessness, and shows up only after age 35. Likely mechanisms are preferences over children, self-esteem, and exposure to working mothers in childhood — not labour-market outcomes or financial constraints. Intergenerational educational mobility, not the degree itself, is what shifts fertility.
data_used: 1970 British Cohort Study (BCS70) — a longitudinal survey of all individuals born in Britain in one week of April 1970, followed into adulthood, with detailed information on parental education, own education, and completed fertility.
policy_relevance: Important context for Hungarian fertility policy (Családtámogatási rendszer, KSH demographic strategy): part of the well-known graduate-fertility gap is not about the degree but about who climbs the educational ladder. Pro-natalist policies aimed at graduate women may underperform if the channel running through 'first in family' status — and the preferences and role-model exposures that come with it — is not addressed. UK evidence; Hungarian replication would strengthen the case, but the mechanism is general.
